Status: Registration opens soon

The Dahilayan Baby Trail 2026 is scheduled for October 11, 2026 in Manolo Fortich, Bukidnon. Organizers have announced three distance categories for the upcoming event: 42K, 21K, and 10K. Registration has not yet opened, but runners have been advised to wait for the next announcement from the official event page.

The race follows the 2025 edition, which was held on October 19 at Dahilayan Gardens and Resort. That event featured 32K, 18K, and 8K categories, with organizers later reporting more than 800 participants. For 2026, the longest distance increases to 42K, while the other categories move to 21K and 10K.

Further details, including registration fees, race inclusions, cut-off times, the exact starting venue, and route information, have not yet been released. Organizers are expected to publish these when registration officially opens.

Photo: Dahilayan BABY TRAIL Facebook Page

]]> Habagat Continues to Bring Heavy Rains Despite Kiyapo Moving Away https://beesayatv.com/habagat-continues-to-bring-heavy-rains-despite-kiyapo-moving-away/ Wed, 29 Jul 2026 01:02:04 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=1138

Status: Advisory in effect

PAGASA reports that although Tropical Storm Kiyapo has moved away from the Philippine Area of Responsibility, the enhanced southwest monsoon (Habagat) continues to affect parts of the country. The weather bureau continues to warn of heavy rainfall in affected areas, with possible flooding and rain-induced landslides.

The advisory remains relevant even after the tropical cyclone has departed, as the southwest monsoon can continue producing periods of moderate to heavy rain over several regions. Local weather conditions may vary depending on location, and residents are advised to monitor the latest PAGASA bulletins.

For hikers and trail users, prolonged rainfall may affect trail conditions, particularly on routes with river crossings, waterfalls, or steep slopes where mud and unstable ground may develop after continuous rain. Those planning outdoor activities are encouraged to check local weather conditions before setting out.

Source: PAGASA. General Flood Advisory and Tropical Cyclone Bulletin. Retrieved July 2026.

]]> How the Smart LTE Layer Is Collected https://beesayatv.com/how-the-smart-lte-layer-is-collected/ Tue, 28 Jul 2026 03:38:31 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=1132

Mobile signal is one of the things that changes most quickly in the mountains.

Some sections of a trail maintain a usable connection for long periods, while others lose service only a short distance later. Because of this, the Smart LTE layer on beesayatv is based entirely on field observations rather than estimates or coverage maps.

Collected During the Hike

Signal measurements are recorded while the hike is taking place.

The data is collected automatically at regular intervals along the documented route, allowing the hike to continue without stopping to record individual readings.

Every point shown on the Trail Atlas represents a location that was physically visited during fieldwork.

Built From Field Observations

After each hike, the recorded measurements are reviewed before being added to the Trail Atlas.

Measurements that fall outside the documented hiking route, such as those collected while travelling to or from the trailhead, may be excluded so that the published layer reflects only the hike itself.

The public map then displays a simplified view showing where a usable Smart LTE connection was observed and where no service was recorded.

A Record of One Visit

Mobile coverage in the mountains is never permanent.

Weather, vegetation, terrain, and changes to the mobile network can all influence signal conditions. For that reason, the Smart LTE layer should be viewed as a record of what was observed during a particular field visit rather than a prediction of future coverage.

Like the documented hiking routes themselves, the Smart LTE layer continues to grow as additional trails are surveyed.

]]> Familiarity Builds Confidence https://beesayatv.com/familiarity-builds-confidence/ Sat, 25 Jul 2026 10:12:15 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=1070

Familiarity Builds Confidence

Many hikers naturally seek new destinations. Exploring unfamiliar trails is part of what makes hiking rewarding. Yet returning to the same trail often offers something just as valuable.

With each visit, uncertainty becomes a little smaller.

Confidence Comes From Repetition

The first visit to a trail often involves constant observation.

Junctions require careful decisions. Dense vegetation may make the route feel uncertain. Small changes in the landscape are difficult to interpret because there is no previous experience to compare them with.

A later visit often feels different. Familiar landmarks, expected climbs, and recognizable turns allow more attention to be given to the conditions that have actually changed.

Familiarity Reveals Change

Trails never remain exactly the same.

Vegetation grows, weather alters the landscape, and farming activity occasionally changes the route. These differences become easier to notice when the trail is already familiar.

Rather than removing uncertainty, familiarity makes it easier to recognize what is unusual.

A Different Kind of Progress

This observation comes from recurring patterns seen across multiple field visits in Cebu.

Exploring new trails remains an important part of field documentation, but revisiting familiar ones often provides a deeper understanding of how a landscape changes over time. Confidence is rarely built through bravery alone. More often, it develops through repeated observation.

]]> Ordinary Places Along the Trail https://beesayatv.com/ordinary-places-along-the-trail/ Thu, 23 Jul 2026 09:41:27 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=996

Most hiking photos naturally focus on the summit, the waterfall, or the viewpoint. Yet on many trails, these places make up only a small part of the day.

Much of the journey passes through community footpaths, farms, quiet forests, narrow mountain paths, and other landscapes that rarely become the focus of hiking media. These places may not be destinations on their own, but they form much of the trail between the better-known landmarks.

They are just as much a part of the documented route.

What Appears Between the Landmarks

Across different hikes, the same ordinary details often reappear.

Fruit-bearing trees beside the trail, grazing livestock, small plants growing from rock crevices, quiet sections of forest, and working agricultural landscapes are encountered far more often than dramatic viewpoints. Individually, none of these moments stand out. Together, they describe what walking through Cebu’s mountains usually looks like.

Rather than recording only the places people expect to see, the fieldwork also documents these quieter parts of the journey.

More Than the Destination

A summit or waterfall may become the most recognizable point along a route, but it represents only a small portion of the walk.

The paths leading there often pass through landscapes that receive little attention despite making up most of the hiking experience. Focusing only on the highlights would leave much of the route undocumented.

Recording these ordinary places helps preserve a more complete picture of how the trail actually unfolds.

Not Every Trail Looks the Same

This observation comes from recurring patterns seen across multiple field visits in Cebu.

Some routes spend long stretches in forest, while others pass through farms or mountain communities. The balance changes from trail to trail, but the examples above reflect features that appear often enough to become a consistent part of the field documentation.

]]> Kara David Documentary Draws Attention to Zambales Dumpsite in Aeta Ancestral Domain https://beesayatv.com/kara-david-documentary-draws-attention-to-zambales-dumpsite-in-aeta-ancestral-domain/ Wed, 22 Jul 2026 10:25:09 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=971

A documentary by journalist Kara David has brought renewed public attention to an open dumpsite operating within the ancestral domain of the Aeta Ambala Indigenous Cultural Community in Subic, Zambales.

The investigation reported that the site had been used for several years without the required environmental permits. Records from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) show that the dumpsite had previously been found in violation of the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, with authorities ordering its closure and the transfer of waste to a sanitary landfill.

The documentary also highlighted concerns raised by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), which recognizes the area as part of the Aeta Ambala ancestral domain. Environmental groups and community members have expressed concern over the potential effects of continued waste disposal on nearby forests, waterways, and the surrounding community.

Following the documentary’s release, I-Witness issued a public statement responding to online claims that questioned its findings. The program said its investigation was based on official government records, field documentation, interviews, and weeks of research, and reaffirmed that it stands by the facts presented in the report.

Photo: GMA Public Affairs / I-Witness

Source: I-Witness official statement; Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR); National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP).

Watch the documentary: Ibinasurang Paraiso by Kara David (I-Witness, YouTube).

]]> DENR Orders Halt After Ten Trees Are Cut at Oslob Plaza https://beesayatv.com/denr-orders-halt-after-ten-trees-are-cut-at-oslob-plaza/ Tue, 21 Jul 2026 00:37:40 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=935

Ten trees at the Oslob town plaza have been completely removed to make way for a proposed sports and cultural complex.

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources in Central Visayas said the Municipality of Oslob had received a special permit covering the removal of 10 identified trees. However, the tree-cutting reportedly proceeded without the required prior coordination and notification to the Community Environment and Natural Resources Office in Argao.

Environmental officials announced that a cease-and-desist order would be issued to stop further tree-cutting and related activity until the permit conditions and other environmental requirements were satisfied. By that time, however, residents reported that all 10 trees had already been cut.

The plaza is also the planned location of a sports and cultural complex opposed by some residents and heritage advocates because of concerns about its effects on the town’s historic surroundings.

Photo: cebu.bomboradyo.com

Source: Claudine Flores, Too late: DENR to stop Oslob tree cutting after all 10 trees are already gone, SunStar Cebu, July 19, 2026.

]]> The People Along the Trail https://beesayatv.com/the-people-along-the-trail/ Sun, 19 Jul 2026 11:41:04 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=872

Many hiking trails in Cebu pass through places where people live and work rather than through isolated forest.

Along these community routes, it is common to see farmers tending crops, residents walking between sitios, children traveling to and from school, or families going about their daily routines. While these moments rarely appear in hiking photos or trail summaries, they are a familiar part of walking many of Cebu’s mountain paths.

Unlike trails used mainly for recreation, these footpaths continue to serve the communities around them every day.

Conversations That Happen Naturally

Walking alone through quieter mountain communities often attracts curiosity.

A greeting along the trail can easily become a short conversation about the surrounding area, the condition of the path, or everyday life in the community. These conversations are not planned interviews, nor are they intended to become the focus of a trail report. They simply happen while passing through places that people call home.

Occasionally, they also provide context that is difficult to find elsewhere.

During one field visit, a resident pointed out that a newly constructed concrete footpath had replaced part of an older walking route, explaining why an earlier GPX track no longer reflected the path most people used. On another hike, a resident shared details about a recent accident along the trail, offering local context that would not have appeared on maps or satellite imagery.

Even when these conversations provide useful background, the trail reports continue to rely primarily on observations made during the field visit itself.

More Than Recreational Routes

These encounters highlight that many community trails serve purposes beyond hiking.

The same paths used by hikers may also connect farms, homes, neighboring sitios, schools, and small roadside stores. For local residents, they are part of everyday life long before they become part of a hiking route.

Passing through these communities is therefore different from walking through an uninhabited landscape. A brief conversation, a returned greeting, or a few minutes spent talking beside the trail reflects that these routes remain active parts of living communities rather than empty corridors between destinations.

Not Every Community Trail Is the Same

Some field visits involve several conversations, while others pass quietly with little more than a wave. The experience naturally varies between communities, the time of day, and who happens to be along the trail.

These examples reflect recurring encounters across multiple community routes in Cebu rather than suggesting that every trail or every visit will unfold in the same way.

]]> Observing the Weekend Hiking Corridor Between Banawa and Pamutan https://beesayatv.com/observing-the-weekend-hiking-corridor-between-banawa-and-pamutan/ Fri, 17 Jul 2026 10:04:01 +0000 https://beesayatv.com/?p=837

Weekend mornings often follow a familiar pattern along the route between Banawa and Barangay Pamutan.

Many hikers begin near Paseo Arcenas before walking through nearby residential areas, passing the Good Shepherd Celestial Garden, and stopping at the Starbuks viewpoint. Some turn back there, while others continue through the Spartan Trail before emerging in Pamutan.

Taken together, these connected segments have become one of the more active hiking corridors documented during weekend field visits.

A Route That Continues Beyond the Trailhead

The journey rarely begins or ends at a single trail.

Instead, it unfolds across different environments. Urban streets gradually give way to residential communities, mountain footpaths, and eventually the rural landscape of Pamutan. The transition is gradual rather than abrupt, making the route feel like a continuous walk instead of a short visit to a single destination.

Although hikers follow different distances and turnaround points, the movement through this corridor remains remarkably consistent from one weekend to another.

The Community Along the Exit

The hike continues even after leaving the Spartan Trail.

Near the trail exit, small refreshment stalls selling buko juice and snacks commonly operate on weekends, serving hikers as they finish the walk. Habal-habal riders also wait nearby, providing transport back toward Labangon for those returning to the city.

These services are not attractions in themselves, but they have become familiar parts of the weekend hiking routine observed along the corridor.

More Than a Single Trail

Pamutan’s connection with outdoor recreation extends beyond everyday weekend hiking.

The barangay regularly hosts hiking and trail-running events, including the Pamutan TrailFest, while the steady weekend flow of hikers through the area suggests that outdoor recreation has become a familiar part of community life rather than an occasional activity.

Viewed together, the route is better understood as a corridor linking neighborhoods, viewpoints, trails, and communities than as a single hiking path.

A Pattern That Continues to Evolve

These observations come from repeated weekend visits along the Banawa–Pamutan route.

The number of hikers, the availability of roadside stalls, and the use of local transport naturally change over time. This article describes the recurring patterns documented during those visits rather than every weekend experience.
